acceptedAnswer.text: Position size = (account size × risk per trade) ÷ (entry price − stop-loss price), rounded down to whole shares. With a ₹1,00,000 account risking 1% (₹1,000), an entry at ₹250 and a stop at ₹240, the stop distance is ₹10 — so you buy 100 shares, deploying ₹25,000 (25% of the account). The stop distance does the real work: the same 1% risk with a ₹5 stop buys 200 shares, while a ₹20 stop buys only 50.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate position size in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 1% rule says never risk more than 1% of your account on a single trade. The math behind it is survival: ten consecutive losses at 1% risk leave you down about 9.6% — annoying but recoverable. Ten losses at 10% risk leave you down 65% — a hole most traders never climb out of. It is a ceiling, not a target.

mainEntity.name: What is the 1% rule in position sizing?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends entirely on your stop, not just the capital. With ₹1,00,000 and 1% risk (₹1,000): entry ₹250 with a ₹240 stop (₹10 distance) gives 100 shares; the same setup with a ₹245 stop (₹5 distance) gives 200 shares. After a ₹40 round-trip brokerage, the cost-aware figure is 96 shares. Anyone quoting a share count without asking for your stop is guessing.

mainEntity.name: How many shares should I buy with ₹1,00,000?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — brokerage comes out of the same risk budget as the stop does. At ₹20 per order, a round trip costs ₹40; on a ₹1,000 risk budget that is 4% of your risk gone before the trade moves. Subtracting the round trip before sizing keeps the risk number honest, especially on small accounts and tight stops.

mainEntity.name: Should I subtract brokerage when calculating position size?

acceptedAnswer.text: Risk per trade is the budget — the rupees you are willing to lose if the stop is hit. Position size is what that budget buys: shares = risk budget ÷ stop distance. Two traders can risk the identical ₹1,000 while holding wildly different sizes, because their stops differ.
